content: Sore throat, fever, headaches, swollen lymph nodes in the neck, characteristic rash[1]
The face is flushed and the rash is red and blanching.[5]
It typically feels like sandpaper and the tongue may be red and bumpy.[1]
The rash usually appears one to two days later, but may appear before or up to seven days following feeling ill.[1]
The skin may feel itchy, but is not painful.[5]
The bacteria are usually spread by people coughing or sneezing.[1]
It can also be spread when a person touches an object that has the bacteria on it and then touches their mouth or nose.[1]
Prevention is by frequent handwashing, not sharing personal items, and staying away from other people when sick.[1]
Antibiotics to combat the streptococcal infection are the mainstay of treatment for scarlet fever.[5]
The antibiotic of choice is Penicillin V which is taken by mouth.[22]
Benzathine penicillin G can be given as a one time intramuscular injection as another alternative if swallowing pills is not possible.[45]
If the person is allergic to the family of antibiotics which both penicillin and amoxicillin are a part of (beta-lactam antibiotics), a first generation cephalosporin is used.[35]
Scarlet fever occurs equally in both males and females.[16]
Children are most commonly infected, typically between 5–15 years old.[21]

The incidence of scarlet fever was reported to be increasing in countries including England, Wales, South Korea, Vietnam, China, and Hong Kong in the 2010s; the cause had not been established as of 2018.[69][70]
There have been several reported outbreaks of the disease in various countries in the past decade.[50]
